cases.explanation: The neighbour asks whether the new game has to reproduce the old one. The children then draw a wider turning square in the middle, choosing a changed layout rather than an exact reproduction.

question.body: What choice do the children make after the neighbour questions whether the new game must reproduce the old one?
options: They stop drawing because their memories conflict.
They use the first child's remembered layout.
They create a changed layout instead of copying the old one.
They recreate the old arrangement exactly from memory.
question.explanation: The neighbour asks whether the new game has to reproduce the old one. The children then draw a wider turning square in the middle, choosing a changed layout rather than an exact reproduction.
question.passage_text: Rain had washed the chalk game from the lane. The children arrived with fresh chalk and began drawing again. One child remembered the old squares as longer; another insisted that the turning square had been on the left. They argued until a passing neighbour asked whether the new game had to reproduce the old one. After a moment, they drew a wider turning square in the middle. Their feet soon covered the fresh lines with pale dust. From her doorway, the neighbour could no longer tell which marks belonged to yesterday and which belonged to the game they had just invented.
